       JEROME AND GAYLYNN SNEED’S REPLY BRIEF ON REMAND ISSUES

          Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed timely submit this Reply Brief on Remand Issues in response

to the Initial Briefs on Remand Issues filed by other parties in this proceeding,1 and would

respectfully show as follows:

                                   I.       EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

          The remand calls for clearer answers on two issues: Issue No. 11, whether the proposed

project is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards; and, Issue No. 13, an estimate of

congestion cost savings. The Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) already evaluated both of these

issues,2 as well as each item Applicants and Staff raise on remand, and its findings should be

upheld:



          1
            See, e.g., Applicants’ Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (Oct. 7, 2026) (hereinafter
Applicants’ Initial Brief on Remand); Commission Staff’s Initial Brief on Remand (Oct. 7, 2026); American Stewards
of Liberty’s Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (Oct. 7, 2026); Save the Lampasas’ Brief
in Response to SOAH Order No. 35 (Oct. 7, 2026).
          2
          See, e.g., Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) at 148–150; Save the Lampasas’ Brief in Response to SOAH
Order No. 35 at 3, 7 (Oct. 7, 2026).

                                                        2
       Issue No. 11: Applicants did not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet state
       or federal reliability standards. Applicants chose a reliability-only theory of need, but
       failed to substantiate it for this project.
           o Applicants made no project-specific showing that Import Path 2 is needed to
               meet any state or federal reliability standard. Applicants and Staff rely on
               system-wide planning studies that never isolated Import Path 2, and Applicants’
               own witness admitted that no study tested the lines independently.
           o Applicants’ reliability theory rests on load projections the ALJs rejected. The
               Permian Basin Reliability Plan’s (“PBRP”) load projections rest on officer letters
               the Commission has since discounted and on an S&P Global forecast that ERCOT
               never deemed credible.
           o Applicants’ reliability theory also rests on a supply premise the ALJs rejected.
               Import Path 2 would carry power west from Central Texas, a region that itself needs
               imports, toward West Texas, where substantial new gas generation is being built.
      Issue No. 13: The record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers
       from Import Path 2. Applicants chose not to provide one, and what Applicants and Staff
       offer instead does not fill the gap.
           o Applicants intentionally omitted evidence of congestion cost savings.
               Applicants disclaimed any economic justification at hearing and still say on remand
               that a congestion analysis is not required.
           o The potential cost savings are nebulous and are not attributable to Import
               Path 2. Staff says only that savings “may” result, and every figure Applicants and
               Staff cite compares entire statewide plans rather than measuring this project.
           o ERCOT’s broader cost-savings estimates evaluate gross savings, not net
               savings. They do not account for the land rights that would be taken or the cost of
               litigating this proceeding.
           o The Commission should not gamble billions of ratepayer dollars on a
               speculative, unquantified chance of savings. Import Path 2 would cost roughly
               $3.7 to $4.3 billion, while its savings to consumers have never been estimated. If
               the Commission is nonetheless inclined to approve the project, it should minimize
               costs to ratepayers by selecting Route 891, which is nearly $9 million less than the
               PFD’s recommended Route 894, bisects the least amount of landowner property
               among the routes of interest, and has the least amount of encroachment on the San
               Saba and Lampasas rivers.

       On remand, the Commission asks the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJ”) to more clearly

and “fully address” Issues Nos. 11 and 13,3 not to reweigh the evidence they have already weighed.

Applicants’ brief4 merely collects evidence the ALJs already considered and simply disagrees with

their fact findings—it does not, and cannot, fill the gaps in the record. For the reasons below, the


       3
           Order Remanding Proceeding to SOAH at 3 (Sept. 18, 2026).

 PFD’s findings are correct and any revised PFD should retain the ALJs’ recommendation that the

Commission deny the Application.


II.     ISSUE NO. 11: APPLICANTS DID NOT ESTABLISH THAT IMPORT PATH 2 IS
          NECESSARY TO MEET STATE OR FEDERAL RELIABILITY STANDARDS

        Applicants fail to establish that the project is necessary to meet state and federal reliability

standards.5 First, no evidence has been presented that the Bell County East to Big Hill portion of

the project or Import Path 2 specifically are necessary to meet any standard. Further, the ALJs

have already considered and rejected both the load and supply projections underlying Applicants’

reliability argument.


        A. No Project-Specific Showing That Import Path 2 Is Needed.

        Applicants offered no evidence that Import Path 2 in particular—as opposed to the 765-kV

plan as a whole—is needed to meet any reliability standard. This distinction is critical, as the

Commission made clear in its order approving the PBRP that each individual CCN proceeding

must establish the need for that project.6

        Applicants’ own witnesses admit that the various components of the PBRP “were studied

together” and that this project was never evaluated individually.7 Applicants and Staff instead rely

on the allegation that Import Path 2 will resolve identified violations “together with” or “in

           Applicants’ Initial Brief on Remand at 4 (Oct. 7, 2026); Commission Staff’s Initial Brief on Remand at 2
(Oct. 7, 2026).

(Oct. 5, 2024).

                                                         4
 conjunction with” the other PBRP projects.8 That argument concedes the point: the study did not

identify any violation that requires Import Path 2 specifically.9

        Furthermore, Applicants’ brief faults the record for containing “no independent analysis or

planning study show[ing] that the plan would still resolve the identified reliability issues without

[Import Path 2]”.10 However, this argument flips the evidentiary burden: Applicants must prove

that Import Path 2 is needed to resolve reliability issues,11 and the missing study is their burden,

not intervenors’.

        Because the Commission ordered each PBRP project to establish need individually, and

because no record evidence isolates Import Path 2 or the Bell County East to Big Hill portion of

the project, Applicants failed to show that this project is necessary to meet any reliability standard.

None of Applicants’ remand arguments fill that evidentiary gap.


        B. Applicants’ Reliability Theory Rests on Load Projections the ALJs Rejected.

        Applicants indicate Import Path 2 is needed to import power into the Permian Basin

because of 1) projected load growth and 2) a lack of local conventional generation.12 However,

the ALJs found the projected load growth underlying Applicants’ justification to be

unsubstantiated by record evidence. In fact, not only the ALJs, but ERCOT, the Commission, and

Staff have all discounted the load forecasts underlying the PBRP and this Application.

2 (Oct. 7, 2026).

(Oct. 7, 2026);

        The Commission acknowledged that ERCOT’s load projection was unsubstantiated and

unlikely to materialize when it approved an adjusted methodology that cut forecasted 2031 summer

peak demand by 27%13 after the PBRP was finalized. Non-oil-and-gas load was the subject of

significant cuts, with the Commission discounting estimates based on transmission service

provider officer letters to a 55.4% realization rate based on ERCOT’s experience that such loads

did not materialize as often as claimed.14 Over half of the PBRP’s projected non-oil-and-gas load

was estimated based on such officer load letters, and Applicants themselves submitted most of the

load represented by officer letters. Yet, their witness admitted “I would not say that we have

verified them,” and Applicants said they “cannot speculate” how the adjusted forecast affects

need.15 Applicants could have offered other evidence of loads actually interconnecting to their

systems in the area, but did not. That omission is telling, and Applicants’ brief fails to address it.

       Applicants’ other proposed findings on oil-and-gas load rely on S&P Global’s

projections,16 which the ALJs found rested on “wish list” scenarios and corporate pledges.17

ERCOT never deemed that forecast credible,18 and projected only 3.1 GW in its long-term forecast

compared to S&P’s projected 10.3 GW by 2030.19 The S&P study was premised on producers

electrifying to meet emissions targets driven by a federal executive order encouraging oil and gas

producers to electrify their operations. However, that executive order was rescinded in January

2025,20 removing a key premise of the projected demand and further undermining the projection.

         The load projections underlying Applicants’ reliability theory are outdated, unverified, or

both, and do not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet any reliability standard. The

“great weight” Applicants demand for ERCOT’s forecast does not change the analysis.21 The

ALJs already found that ERCOT’s recommendation is not entitled to great weight under the rule

because its load forecast was not substantiated, and that even if great weight were applied, the

weight of the evidence against Applicants is greater.22


        C. Applicants’ Reliability Theory Also Rests on a Supply Premise the ALJs
           Rejected.

        The second premise, a lack of local generation, fails as well. This project would move

power across the state, but Applicants have the “from there” and “to here” reversed. Import Path

2 is designed to move power from Central Texas to West Texas, yet in reality new gas generation

is being built in West Texas while Central Texas needs imports.

        Applicants’ witness says there is “ample generation elsewhere on the system”23 available

to be imported to the Permian Basin region, but neither Applicants nor ERCOT analyzed Central

Texas’s net generation position or whether Central Texas could serve its own data-center and other

growth and still export power west.24 Meanwhile, ERCOT’s 2025 RTP says that Central Texas,

where the East Bell County to Big Hill line starts, itself “faces the challenge of needing additional

import capability.”25

         At the other end of the line, the generation picture has changed. The PBRP’s premise was

a “lack of conventional generation in the Permian Basin,” about 2.8 GW at the time.26 Since then,

37 planned or announced gas generation projects in the Permian Basin, West Texas, and the

Panhandle total about 39.5 GW, exceeding the load the import paths were designed to serve.27 The

ALJs found that the new West Texas gas generation is a credible alternative that could reduce or

eliminate the need for Import Path 2.28

        Applicants’ brief’s emphasis on “bidirectional” flow does not change this.29 Applicants

call the ALJs’ finding that Import Path 2 projects will import power from across the state of Texas

for transit westward into the Permian Basin30 “flatly incorrect.”31 But the PBRP justified the

import paths by imports into the Permian Basin, not exports, as Staff’s witness confirmed.32

Because the power Import Path 2 would carry westward is neither shown to exist at Bell County

East nor needed given new West Texas generation, the line would not increase the supply of power

to West Texas, and the supply premise of Applicants’ reliability theory fails.

        For all three reasons—no project-specific showing, unsupported load projections, and a

failed supply premise—Applicants did not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet any

state or federal reliability standard.

  III.      ISSUE NO. 13: THE RECORD CONTAINS NO ESTIMATE OF CONGESTION
                  COST SAVINGS TO CONSUMERS FROM IMPORT PATH 2

          The record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers from Import Path

2, because Applicants chose not to provide one. What Applicants and Staff offer in its place does

not fill that gap: their figures are nebulous and not attributable to Import Path 2, they measure

gross savings rather than net savings or benefits, and they cannot justify the billions of dollars

Import Path 2 would cost ratepayers.


          A. Applicants Indicated That They Intentionally Omitted Evidence of Congestion
             Cost Savings.

          No estimate of congestion cost savings exists because Applicants deliberately chose not to

provide one. Applicants’ Initial Brief answered Issue No. 13 only by stating that the project “is

not justified based on economic criteria,”33 and Applicants called the omission of congestion cost

savings “intentional and immaterial.”34 On remand, Applicants still say a congestion cost savings

analysis is “not required,”35 and Staff says one “is not necessary.”36 Both concede that no estimate

exists.        Applicants nonetheless ask the ALJs to amend their findings of fact to recognize

“voluminous” evidence of consumer benefits.37 But Issue No. 13 asks for an estimate of savings

from these facilities, and vague “benefits” do not constitute an estimate. The ALJs correctly found

that the record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers.38

        B. The Potential Cost Savings Are Nebulous and Are Not Attributable to Import
          Path 2.

       The potential savings Applicants and Staff purport to exist are nebulous at best, and none

of them are identified as attributable to Import Path 2. Staff indicates only that congestion cost

savings “may result.”39 Staff’s own figures allege that, compared with building none of the plans,

the entire statewide 765 kV plan lowers consumer energy cost by $63 million in 203440—none of

which is identified as specifically attributed to Import Path 2. ERCOT’s $94 million congestion

rent (2034), $172 million congestion rent (2039), and $229 million (annual) consumer energy cost

savings figures compare the entire 765 kV plan to the 345 kV plan; ERCOT never ran a comparison

comparing the 765 kV plan with and without Import Path 2.41 Applicants’ other figures—$270

million in annual savings, $890 million in avoided outage costs, 1,443 miles of avoided upgrades,

and 560 GWh in reduced losses—likewise compare the entire 765 kV plan to the 345 kV

alternative.42 No figure Applicants allege is identified as tied to Import Path 2 or the East Bell

County to Big Hill project specifically, and none is a congestion cost savings estimate.


       C. ERCOT’s Cost-Savings Estimates Evaluate Gross Savings, Not Net Savings.

       Even ERCOT’s general estimates evaluate gross savings, not net savings. ERCOT’s

economic study measures market metrics only: production cost, consumer energy cost, and

congestion rent.43 It does not account for the invaluable land rights that will be infringed upon

along a 214 to 244-mile right-of-way,44 or for the millions of dollars spent litigating this

 proceeding. Even a project-specific savings estimate, had one existed, would overstate the net

benefit to consumers.


         D. The Commission Should Not Gamble Billions of Ratepayer Dollars on a
            Speculative, Unquantified Chance of Savings.

         Import Path 2’s estimated cost is roughly $3.7 to $4.3 billion.45 Those costs are certain and

borne by ratepayers. The offsetting savings attributable to Import Path 2, however, have never

been estimated, and Staff’s figures put the entire statewide plan’s consumer savings at only $63

million to $156 million a year.46

         If the Commission is nonetheless inclined to approve the project, it should minimize the

risk of cost increases to ratepayers by selecting Route 891—nearly $9 million less expensive than

the route recommended in the PFD and the second-least-expensive Route of Interest.47 Route 891

additionally minimizes infringement on landowners’ properties, bisecting the least amount of

landowner property of any other Route of Interest in the case and minimizing infringement of

property rights. In particular, not choosing Links G13 or G51 would, in addition to saving money,

significantly reduce the damage to the Lampasas River watershed, and reduce damages to

landowners by significantly reducing the number of properties which are bisected, or, in the

Sneeds’ case, trisected. It is not surprising that Staff missed this point, through no fault of Staff’s

witness Mr. Poole or others. The route was not included in Mr. Poole’s substantive analysis and

Staff did not have time (due to the accelerated schedule) to read the testimony of either Mr. Sneed

substation costs. PFD at 5.

 or his expert, Ms. Karen Hubbard, at the time Staff made the decision to include Links G13 and

        Ratepayers should not bear certain, multi-billion-dollar costs for potential nebulous savings

no one has quantified. The record is clear on Issue No. 13: Applicants chose not to quantify any

congestion cost savings, and the studies they rely on similarly fail to quantify the savings

attributable to Import Path 2 or the Bell County East to Big Hill portion of the project.


                                           IV.      CONCLUSION

        The record answers both remand issues against Applicants. On Issue No. 11, Applicants

did not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet any state or federal reliability standard.

On Issue No. 13, the record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers. In

particular, not choosing Links G13 or G51 would, in addition to saving money, significantly reduce

the damage to the Lampasas River watershed, and reduce damages to landowners by significantly

reducing the number of properties which are bisected, or, in the Sneeds’ case, trisected. Jerome

and Gaylynn Sneed therefore respectfully request that the ALJs issue a supplemental PFD

answering Issue Nos. 11 and 13 consistent with this brief, retain their recommendation that the

Commission deny the Application, and grant the Sneeds any other relief to which they are entitled.

          Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed timely submit this Reply Brief on Remand Issues in response

                                     I.       EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

          The remand calls for clearer answers on two issues: Issue No. 11, whether the proposed

project is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards; and, Issue No. 13, an estimate of

congestion cost savings.         The Proposal for Decision ("PFD") already evaluated both of these

issues,2 as well as each item Applicants and Staff raise on remand, and its findings should be

upheld:

II.     ISSUE NO. 11: APPLICANTS DID NOT ESTABLISH THAT IMPORT PATH 2 IS
          NECESSARY TO MEET STATE OR FEDERAL RELIABILITY STANDARDS

        Applicants fail to establish that the project is necessary to meet state and federal reliability

standards.5 First, no evidence has been presented that the Bell County East to Big Hill portion of

the project or Import Path 2 specifically are necessary to meet any standard. Further, the ALJs

have already considered and rejected both the load and supply projections underlying Applicants'

reliability argument.


        A. No Proiect-Specific Showing That Import Path 2 Is Needed.

        Applicants offered no evidence that Import Path 2 in particular-as opposed to the 765-kV

plan as a whole-is needed to meet any reliability standard. This distinction is critical, as the

Commission made clear in its order approving the PBRP that each individual CCN proceeding

must establish the need for that project . 6

        Applicants' own witnesses admit that the various components of the PBRP "were studied

together" and that this project was never evaluated individually.7 Applicants and Staffinstead rely

on the allegation that Import Path 2 will resolve identified violations "together with" or "in

        Furthermore, Applicants' brief faults the record for containing "no independent analysis or

[Import Path 2]" 10 However, this argument flips the evidentiary burden: Applicants must prove

None of Applicants' remand arguments fill that evidentiary gap.

the ALJs found the projected load growth underlying Applicants' justification to be

unsubstantiated by record evidence. In fact, not only the ALJs, but ERCOT, the Commission, and

Staff have all discounted the load forecasts underlying the PBRP and this Application.

         The load projections underlying Applicants' reliability theory are outdated, unverified, or

both, and do not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet any reliability standard. The

"great weight" Applicants demand for ERCOT's forecast does not change the analysis.21 The

ALJs already found that ERCOT' s recommendation is not entitled to great weight under the rule

because its load forecast was not substantiated, and that even if great weight were applied, the

weight of the evidence against Applicants is greater.22


        C. Applicants' Reliability Theory Also Rests on a Supply Premise the ALJs
           Reiected.

        The second premise, a lack of local generation, fails as well. This project would move

power across the state, but Applicants have the "from there" and "to here" reversed. Import Path

2 is designed to move power from Central Texas to West Texas, yet in reality new gas generation

is being built in West Texas while Central Texas needs imports.

        Applicants' witness says there is "ample generation elsewhere on the system"23 available

to be imported to the Permian Basin region, but neither Applicants nor ERCOT analyzed Central

Texas' s net generation position or whether Central Texas could serve its own data-center and other

growth and still export power west.24 Meanwhile, ERCOT's 2025 RTP says that Central Texas,

where the East Bell County to Big Hillline starts, itself "faces the challenge of needing additional

import capability."25

         At the other end ofthe line, the generation picture has changed. The PBRP' s premise was

a "lack of conventional generation in the Permian Basin," about 2.8 GW at the time.26 Since then,

37 planned or announced gas generation projects in the Permian Basin, West Texas, and the

Panhandle total about 39.5 GW, exceeding the load the import paths were designed to serve.27 The

ALJs found that the new West Texas gas generation is a credible alternative that could reduce or

eliminate the need for Import Path 2.28

        Applicants' brief's emphasis on "bidirectional" flow does not change this.29 Applicants

call the ALJs' finding that Import Path 2 projects will import power from across the state of Texas

for transit westward into the Permian Basin30 "flatly incorrect."31 But the PBRP justified the

import paths by imports into the Permian Basin, not exports, as Staff' s witness confirmed.32

Because the power Import Path 2 would carry westward is neither shown to exist at Bell County

East nor needed given new West Texas generation, the line would not increase the supply of power

to West Texas, and the supply premise of Applicants' reliability theory fails.

        For all three reasons-no project-specific showing, unsupported load projections, and a

failed supply premise--Applicants did not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet any

state or federal reliability standard.

  III.      ISSUE NO. 13: THE RECORD CONTAINS NO ESTIMATE OF CONGESTION
                  COST SAVINGS TO CONSUMERS FROM IMPORT PATH 2

          The record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers from Import Path

2, because Applicants chose not to provide one. What Applicants and Staff offer in its place does

not fill that gap: their figures are nebulous and not attributable to Import Path 2, they measure

gross savings rather than net savings or benefits, and they cannot justify the billions of dollars

Import Path 2 would cost ratepayers.


          A. Applicants Indicated That Thev Intentionally Omitted Evidence of Congestion
             Cost Savings.

          No estimate of congestion cost savings exists because Applicants deliberately chose not to

provide one. Applicants' Initial Brief answered Issue No. 13 only by stating that the project "is

not justified based on economic criteria,"33 and Applicants called the omission of congestion cost

savings "intentional and immaterial."34 On remand, Applicants still say a congestion cost savings

analysis is "not required,"35 and Staff says one "is not necessary."36 Both concede that no estimate

exists.    Applicants nonetheless ask the ALJs to amend their findings of fact to recognize

" voluminous " evidence of consumer benefits . 37 But Issue No . 13 asks for an estimate of savings

from these facilities, and vague "benefits" do not constitute an estimate. The ALJs correctly found

that the record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers.38

        B. The Potential Cost Savings Are Nebulous and Are Not Attributable to Import
          Path 2.

       The potential savings Applicants and Staff purport to exist are nebulous at best, and none

of them are identified as attributable to Import Path 2. Staff indicates only that congestion cost

savings "may result."39 Staff' s own figures allege that, compared with building none ofthe plans,

the entire statewide 765 kV plan lowers consumer energy cost by $63 million in 203440-none of

which is identified as specifically attributed to Import Path 2. ERCOT' s $94 million congestion

rent (2034), $172 million congestion rent (2039), and $229 million (annual) consumer energy cost

savings figures compare the entire 765 kV plan to the 345 kV plan; ERCOT never ran a comparison

comparing the 765 kV plan with and without Import Path 2.41 Applicants' other figures-$270

million in annual savings, $890 million in avoided outage costs, 1,443 miles of avoided upgrades,

and 560 GWh in reduced losses-likewise compare the entire 765 kV plan to the 345 kV

alternative.42 No figure Applicants allege is identified as tied to Import Path 2 or the East Bell

County to Big Hill project specifically, and none is a congestion cost savings estimate.

                                           IV.      CONCLUSION

         The record answers both remand issues against Applicants. On Issue No. 11, Applicants

did not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet any state or federal reliability standard.

On Issue No. 13, the record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings to consumers. In

particular, not choosing Links G13 or G51 would, in addition to saving money, significantly reduce

the damage to the Lampasas River watershed, and reduce damages to landowners by significantly

reducing the number of properties which are bisected, or, in the Sneeds' case, trisected. Jerome

and Gaylynn Sneed therefore respectfully request that the ALJs issue a supplemental PFD

answering Issue Nos. 11 and 13 consistent with this brief, retain their recommendation that the

Commission deny the Application, and grant the Sneeds any other relief to which they are entitled.
